findings.claim: Always ground your answer in the specific problem given — examiners reward precise application, not generic definitions.
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. No AQA source states that examiners reward applied answers over generic definitions. The advice itself is sound, so it should be stated as advice and not attributed to examiners.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented examiner or mark-scheme claims. Spec 3.1.1 sets the content but says nothing about how examiners credit answers.

findings.claim: A flowchart for a loop has an arrow that curves back upward from the “No” exit of the diamond to an earlier step.
findings.truth: The loop-back arrow can leave either exit. It depends on how the condition is worded. 'Is count > 10?' loops back on No; 'Is count <= 10?' loops back on Yes. Teaching that it is always the 'No' exit is a misconception stated as fact, and it can make a student take the wrong branch in a flowchart-completion or trace question.
findings.evidence: Recomputation from first principles; spec 3.1.1 requires students to represent algorithms as flowcharts and to trace them.

findings.truth: AQA standard pseudo-code writes 'greater than or equal to' as ≥, not as >=. The same lesson already uses ≠ in its WHILE example, so the block is internally inconsistent. The sibling unit computer-science-aqa/programming writes 'IF score ≥ 70 THEN' and 'IF age ≥ 16 ...'.
findings.evidence: Spec 3.1.1: 'Any exam question where students are given pseudo-code will use the AQA standard version.' Spec 3.2: 'Exams will always present algorithms using the current version of the AQA pseudo-code.' Cross-check against computer-science-aqa/programming L01 and L02.

findings.claim: In the exam, trace-table questions are worth 4 marks and are one of the most commonly dropped mark areas. The two most frequent errors are:
findings.truth: A fabricated fixed tariff plus an unevidenced examiner-report claim. AQA 8525 trace-table questions carry a range of marks; no source fixes them at 4, and no source ranks them as a most-dropped area.
findings.evidence: Spec 2.2 Paper 1: 'A mix of multiple choice, short answer and longer answer questions'. No tariff is fixed to a question type anywhere in the spec.

findings.claim: For trace-table questions (4 marks), complete every cell for every iteration
findings.truth: The same invented fixed tariff as F4. The advice stands once the '(4 marks)' is removed.

findings.claim: Each paired comparison earns more marks than describing one algorithm then the other separately.
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme claim. AQA does not publish a rule that paired comparisons score higher than parallel descriptions. The structural advice is good practice and should be stated as such.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented mark-scheme claims. Spec 3.1.3 only requires students to 'compare and contrast linear and binary search algorithms'.

findings.claim: Avoid listing all of bubble sort’s features then all of merge sort’s — direct comparisons earn more marks.
findings.truth: The same invented mark-scheme claim as F6, in the sorting lesson.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented mark-scheme claims. Spec 3.1.4 requires only 'compare and contrast merge sort and bubble sort algorithms'.

findings.claim: but it becomes impractical for lists with more than a few hundred items
findings.truth: An invented numeric threshold, and it is wrong. Bubble sort on a few hundred items needs at most a few tens of thousands of comparisons, which any computer does in a fraction of a second. The correct GCSE statement is the plain-English one: bubble sort becomes far too slow as the list grows large.
findings.evidence: Recomputation: 500 items gives at most 499 x 500 / 2 = 124,750 comparisons. Spec 3.1.2: 'Formal comparisons of algorithmic efficiency are not required' and comparisons refer to time efficiency only.

findings.claim: All four lessons carry a sixth practice question typed '8 marks — Extended Response' (L1 'Evaluate the benefits of decomposition...', L2 trace table vs visual inspection, L3 time efficiency, L4 merge sort at 500 million records).
findings.truth: Algorithms is 3.1, so it is examined on Paper 1. The spec describes Paper 1 as 'a mix of multiple choice, short answer and longer answer questions'; 'extended response' is named only for Paper 2 (3.3 to 3.8, including SQL). Options: (a) relabel to '8 marks — Longer Answer' in this unit only; (b) relabel across the whole AQA computer-science subject, since the same type string appears in computer-science-aqa/programming (also Paper 1 content); (c) leave it, because '8 marks — Extended Response' is a fleet-wide house label rather than a claim about AQA's own question naming. RECOMMEND (b): the label is only wrong where the content sits on Paper 1, and both AQA CS Paper 1 units are in the retro queue, so fix them together rather than leaving the subject half-relabelled. The questions themselves are good practice and should be kept; only the type string changes.
findings.evidence: Spec 2.2, Paper 1 and Paper 2 'Questions' descriptions; spec 2.1 places 3.1 in Paper 1. Type strings counted across scripts/_retrofc/units/computer-science-aqa__algorithms and computer-science-aqa__programming (4 occurrences each).
findings.ruling: NOTE: '8 marks - Extended Response' label on Paper 1 content left for the question-type relabel sweep (apply across both AQA CS Paper 1 units).

findings.claim: Question 5 is typed '6 marks — Write a Subroutine' but asks the student to 'Write AQA pseudo-code for a program that asks the user for ten numbers, one at a time, and outputs their total.'
findings.truth: The question asks for a program, not a subroutine, so the label does not match the task. Not edited: '6 marks — Write a Subroutine' is the established house type across the AQA computer-science subject (5 further occurrences in computer-science-aqa/programming), so a one-lesson change would break subject consistency. Worth a subject-level tidy alongside F9.
findings.evidence: Type strings counted across the two AQA computer-science unit dirs in scripts/_retrofc/units.

findings.claim: Binary search worked example, Step 2: 'Search area indices 5–8. Middle index = 6, value = 27.'
findings.truth: The trace is correct and self-consistent: (5 + 8) DIV 2 = 6, matching AQA's round-down midpoint convention, and the whole example (3 comparisons, found at index 5) checks out. The lesson never states the rounding rule, so a student who computes 6.5 and rounds up gets index 7 and a different trace. Not edited: nothing is wrong, only unstated.
findings.evidence: Hand trace of [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35] for target 23; midpoint recomputed at every step.

findings.claim: 'Compare items at positions 1 and 2 — swap if needed. Compare positions 2 and 3' and 'largest item (8) is now in position 5'.
findings.truth: Lesson 4 counts positions from 1 while lesson 3 counts array indices from 0 ('use 0 as the first index'), and AQA pseudo-code arrays are 0-indexed. 'Position' is ordinary English and is not wrong, so no edit; flagged only because the unit mixes the two conventions.
findings.evidence: Spec 3.1.1 on AQA standard pseudo-code; internal comparison of L3 and L4.

findings.claim: String literals in the pseudo-code reference are written with curly double quotes: OUTPUT “Pass”, WHILE answer ≠ “quit”, UNTIL answer = “quit”.
findings.truth: AQA standard pseudo-code encloses string literals in single quotes. Not edited: students may use any pseudo-code in their answers, the quote style costs no marks, and reflowing three code blocks risks more than it fixes. Worth folding into a subject-level pseudo-code style pass.
findings.evidence: Spec 3.1.1 and 3.2 on the AQA standard pseudo-code; internal comparison with the ≠ already used in the same block.

summary: Every algorithm in the unit was hand-run and is correct: the L2 trace table (FOR 1 TO 4, output 10) and its practice trace (output 12), the L3 binary search of [3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35] for 23 (3 comparisons, index 5, round-down midpoint applied consistently), the L3 practice binary search for 'Daly' (index 3, found in 1 comparison), the L4 bubble sort of [5,3,8,1,4] pass by pass, its practice bubble sort of [6,2,9,4,1] pass by pass, and the L4 merge sort split and merge trees for [38,27,43,3,9,82,10]. All 20 knowledge-check keys, including the four match-up orders, are correct, as are the comparison counts (1,000 items to at most 10; one million to at most 20; 8 items to at most 4). The defects are all in the exam-claim layer: three invented examiner or mark-scheme claims, one invented fixed tariff repeated in two fields, one invented efficiency threshold, one flowchart misconception, and one AQA pseudo-code operator mismatch.
